Zero Prospectives, Zero Modals, and Modo-Temporal Interactions in nsyilxcn (Okanagan Salish)* John Lyon University of British Columbia - Okanagan Abstract: This paper motivates a zero prospective marker for nsyilxcn, in complementary distribution with overt markers mi and k-. This paper also examines interactions between tense /aspect, and epistemic cəm̓/cmay and bouletic cakʷ. I suggest that cakʷ fits the profile of a bouletic mood marker (Matthewson 2010) as opposed to a modal proper , and that there is a zero circumstantial modal in nsyilxcn (Matthewson 2013 for Gitksan, Hannon 2025 for nɬeʔkepmxcín). Notably, the zero modal and zero prospective co -occur, which means that a given sentence can be ambiguous between a prospective modal reading and a non -prospective non-modal reading. I show that context is criti cal in disambiguating these two readings.
Keywords: aspect, modals, modo-temporal interaction, mood, Southern Interior Salish

nsyilxcn (a.k.a. Okanagan, Southern Interior Salish ) is unusual among Salish languages in that prospective marking can often be omitted in future-oriented contexts (N. Mattina 1999). It is also the case that prospective sentences, whether overtly marked as such or not, sometimes have modal interpretations. In light of this, this paper has two main goals.

The first goal is to motivate a morphologically zero prospective marker in nsyilxcn. The zero prospective marker alternates with two overt prospective marking strategies , particle mi and inflectional k-----(mix)aʔx/(a)m. The second goal is to examine the semantic interaction between epistemic and circumstantial modals and the tense/aspect system, with particular attention paid to zero- and overt ly-marked prospectives. This paper aims to fill a gap in our understanding of prospectives across Salish, and to provide some understanding of modo-temporal interactions from the Southern Interior Salish perspective. The focus here is on empirical patterns as opposed to formal analysis, though I do take tentative steps towards an analysis . The paper is structured as follows:

form: Section 2 reviews evidence for a morphologically zero and semantically underspecified grammatical tense in nsyilxcn, and provides some background on sentential aspect (see Lyon 2024, Lyon in prep, for a more detailed discussion). Section 3 compares sentences with overt prospective marking to future-oriented sentences which lack prospective marking altogether . I show that t he zero prospective is generally judged felicitous in contexts for which the futurity of the event is mutually understood, though it is sometimes rejected out of context, or in contexts for which there is a competing, pragmatically plausible non -prospective interpretation . Section 4 builds on Menzies’ (2013) study of nsyilxcn modals in re-examining epistemic cəm̓/cmay and bouletic cakʷ with respect to the temporal-aspectual system. In 4.1, I show that epistemic cəm̓/cmay can have a present, past, or future temporal orientation depending on the sentential aspect of the predicate (Rullmann & Matthewson 2018). In 4.2, I show that bouletic cakʷ can co-occur with epistemic cəm̓/cmay (Menzies 2013), and that cakʷ cannot generally occur in circumstantial contexts which do not reflect the goals/desires of the speaker. Since the environments in which cakʷ is used appear to largely overlap with subjunctive marking in St’át’imcets (Matthewson 2010), and cakʷ can co- occur with both prospective and non-prospective aspects, which is unexpected for a circumstantial modal (Condoravdi 2002, Rullmann & Matthewson 2018), I propose that cakʷ is a bouletic mood marker (Portner 1997, Matthewson 2010), rather than a modal proper. Finally, since circumstantial modal contexts do not require cakʷ, and typically use only overt or zero prospective aspect , I propose that there is a zero circumstantial modal in nsyilxcn (Matthewson et. al, 2022; Hannon 2025). Section 5 provides a summary, and an informal sketch of an analysis, and outlines several points for future research.

Section 2.1 reviews evidence for a zero grammatical tense . S ection 2.2 provides a summary description and analysis of sentential aspect, aside from prospective aspect which is presented separately in section 3.

nsyilxcn tense is morphologically zero (N. Mattina 1999, Dunham 2011, Lyon 2024, Lyon in prep). This means that a given sentence may in principle be interpreted as having past, present or future temporal reference. Temporal reference is established through one or more of the following strategies: (i) default interpretations based on aktionsart , (ii) discourse context, (iii) temporal adverbials (N. Mattina 1999), (iv) viewpoint aspectual restrictions in a few cases. For example, the perfective ditransitive accomplishment predicate ʔiɬ-[ɬ]t- eat-REDR- ‘to eat something belonging to someone’ defaults to a completive reading (i.e. ‘maximal’) with a past temporal reference (1a), but also allows for ongoing reading (i.e. ‘non -maximal’) with present temporal reference (1b), and future temporal reference in the context of a future adverbial (1c). Perfective accomplishments imply without entailing maximality, which enables the ongoing event reading in (1b) (Bar-el 2005, Lyon 2024, Lyon in prep).1,2

Despite this, both future temporal reference as well a s a prospective orientation at a past or present temporal reference point are generally the more marked interpretations. In the absence of either prospective marking, a future temporal adverbial, or a contextual clue indicating an action will happen in the immediate future, a sentence is much less likely to be accepted as having future temporal reference or a prospective orientation . Sentential aspect in nsyilxcn consists of three distinct layers, each of which contributes a distinct semantics to the overall meaning of the verb, as schematized in Figure 1 (Lyon 2024, in prep). The innermost ‘inclusion aspect’ layer attaches directly to a verb stem and consists of an alternation between a zero perfective and an imperfective prefix əc-. Next, extended -now aspect (a.k.a. continuative, or ‘extended’ for short) s----(mi)x/(a)m6 alternates with a zero non-extended aspect.7 Lastly, prospective k----(mix)aʔx/(a)m (and its zero variant) alternates with a zero non-prospective marker. The prefixal portions of all three markers can occur in sequence, as in (6). They may also occur independently of one another with the exception that prospective k- requires either extended- now s- and/or imperfective əc-. Inclusion aspect is illustrated above in §2.1, so I now review extended-now aspect. Extended-now aspect is similar to a perfect in the sense that it contributes an extended -now timespan which contains the event run-time as a proper or non-proper sub-interval (Lyon 2024, in prep). Similarly to a perfect, a semantic contrast is apparent, based on whether the underlying predicate is imperfective or perfective (Pancheva 2003).
‘When Hailey came in, I was in the middle of dancing.’
‘When Hailey came in, I was done dancing.’ (Delphine Derickson-Armstrong | CF)

Extended-now aspect imposes singularity over eventuality parts (Lyon 2024, in prep). This means that true habitual readings are not possible for extended imperfectives . Compare the base imperfective in (8a) with the extended-now imperfective in (8b).
Context: You’re talking about some of the things you’d typically do when you were younger.
‘I used to help my aunt when I was young.’ (Dave Michele | VF)
‘I was (continuously) helping my aunt when I was young.’ (Dave Michele | CF)

Further, in contrast to non-extended perfectives which allow ongoing event readings (9a, cf. 1b), with extended-now perfectives an event must not be ongoing at a reference time (9b). Lyon (in prep) treats nsyilxcn extended-now aspect as introducing maximality over event stages (Altschuler 2014). The perfective requires an event stage, whereas the imperfective only requires an event part, not necessarily an event stage, hence extended aspect will only necessarily require maximality with perfectives. Extended imperfectives are typically interpreted as non-maximal, though these can also have maximal readings if the event has ceased at or before speech time.
Context: You know that Mary has started writing a story, and are not sure if she finished.
‘Mary wrote a story, maybe she is still writing it.’ (Delphine Derickson-Armstrong | VF)

Extended-now aspect also attaches to bare states. These typically have non-maximal (‘universal’) readings at a reference time (10) though maximal, experiential readings are also possible (e.g. Have you been hungry? ). Since maximality is not required in these cases , in contrast to eventive predicates (e.g. 9b), Lyon (in prep) proposes that states do not take the zero perfective. If there were a zero perfective in (10), for example, then the prediction is that extended aspect should enforce a maximal reading, but this is not the case.
Context: Dave addressing a student who is eating something in class.
‘Goodness, are you still hungry?’ (Dave Michele, VF)

Overall, the contrast between the existential readings found with extended-now perfectives, and the universal readings found with extended-now states and imperfectives suggests that extended-now aspect is in some ways similar to a perfect (cf. Iatridou et. al 2001, Pancheva 2003). Indeed, extended-now interpretations emerge in the context of adverbials which can take on a since meaning. The since clause in (11a) entails that the imperfective event occurred at least once during the time span that stretches between the time when John was 12 years old and speech time. The quasi-habitual reading in (11a) (not possible in the absence of the since clause) is due to the since clause introducing existential quantification over events within an extended now time span (Iatridou et al 2001). The since interpretation is generally only available with extended predicates (11a, not 11b), which follows if extended predicates introduce an ‘extended-now’ time span, which the since clause then references.

Unlike the English perfect, nsyilxcn extended-now aspect is not inherently retrospective. Example (12a), classified by A. Discourse context plays a critical role in disambiguating the zero marker, as I show below.

In reviewing nsyilxcn sentential aspect in this section, we have seen two separate environments which support the idea of a zero prospective: base transitives (4a) and extended -now perfectives (12). The next section illustrates other environments which seem to involve a zero prospective.

This section introduces the two overt prospective marking strategies (mi and k-) while comparing and contrasting these with the zero prospective. While some speakers more strongly prefer overt prospective marking (DM) than other speakers (DD,SM), all accept and sometimes volunteer zero prospectives. In what follows I show that prospective marking may be omitted in contexts for which the futurity of the event is mutually understood.

Sentences with a future temporal orientation commonly have overt prospective marking. This is realized by either a particle mi or inflectional k-....(mix)aʔx/ám (abbreviated as k- in the prose) marking on the predicate. In all other syntactic environments for which prospective aspect is overtly marked , k- may surface on t he predicate. k- nearly always co -occurs with an s- prefix. There are three different types of k-s- constructions, morphosyntactically speaking (see A. Mattina 1993). First, intransitives with indicative agreement in main or subordinate clauses have a suffixal portion –(mix)aʔx (19a), with -mix surfacing with phonologically weak stems. Second, transitives in main or subordinate clauses take ergative agreement, except in 1 st and 2nd person (and sometimes 3 rd) singular where agreement is possessive (19b) and an –(a)m suffix surfaces, with -a surfacing with phonologically weak stems. Third, intransitives in subordinate clauses may take possessive agreement without any aspectual suffix (19c). (19a-b) involve extended-now aspect, while I assume that (1 9c) does not, though further work is needed here.13

This section examines interactions between sentential aspect and modality. I survey two particles: epistemic cəm̓/cmay (section 4.1) and bouletic cakʷ and a range of other non-overtly marked circumstantial contexts (section 4.2).18 As a terminological preliminary, I follow Condoravdi (2002) and Rullmann & Matthewson (2018:2-3) in using temporal perspective (‘TP’) to describe the time at which the conversational background of a modal is evaluated, and temporal orientation (‘TO’) to describe the relation between temporal perspective and the time of the event. I assume that a modal’s temporal perspective is determined by a higher tense morpheme (Rullmann & Matthewson 2018), which in nsyilxcn is always null.

Epistemic modals reflect the certainty of a speaker with respect to his knowledge (e.g. English “might/must” under one reading). In nsyilxcn, epistemic possibility is indicated through cəm̓/cmay.19 In the absence of overt prospective marking, a modal sentence containing cəm̓/cmay may have any temporal orientation, depending on the context. (3 7) for example may have a past (37a) or future temporal orientation (37b).

This section has shown that the temporal orientation of epistemic cəm̓/cmay depends on the aspectual properties of the inflected predicate. This means that in order for the modal to have a future TO in the absence of overt prospective marking, a zero prospective must be providing th at temporal orientation. Additionally, it was shown that for prospective sentences without cəm̓/cmay, an epistemic interpretation is not available . This suggests overall that nsyilxcn prospectives are non-modal prospectives, and that there is no zero epistemic modal in the absence of cəm̓/cmay.

This section examines the interaction between circumstantial modality and temporal pers pective and orientation in nsyilxcn, but also attempts to reframe previous understandings of circumstantial modality (Menzies 2013). In §4.2.1, I show that a subset of circumstantial contexts occur with a bouletic particle cakʷ, which Menzies (2013) treats as modal. cakʷ appears to have a future temporal orientation in these cases. In §4.2.2., I show that cakʷ may also be used with non-prospective aspects. Circumstantial modals, by hypothesis always have a future temporal orientation (Rullmann & Matthewson 2018 ). This means that cakʷ cannot be receiving it’s temporal orientation from sentential aspect, in contrast to cəm̓/cmay discussed in §4.1. In §4.2.3, I show that c ircumstantial readings are possible in the absence of any modal particle . Additionally, cakʷ may co-occur with epistemic cəm̓/cmay and is used in contexts for which subjunctive marking applies in other Salish languages (St’át’imcets , Matthewson 2010) . For th ese reasons, I suggest that there is a zero circumstantial modal in nsyilxcn (Matthewson et. al, 2022; Hannon 2025), and that cakʷ is in fact a bouletic mood marker which is consistent with either an epistemic or circumstantial modal base. §4.2.4 provides a brief summary.

form: This section has shown that the zero/overt prospective marker can co-occur with bouletic particle cakʷ in a range of circumstantial modal contexts (§4.2.1). cakʷ can also occur with non-prospective aspects. This is unexpected if cakʷ is a circumstantial modal, given that circumstantial modals always have a future orientation, and that modal orientation is determined by viewpoint aspect (Rullmann & Matthewson 2018) (§4.2.2). cakʷ however can co-occur with epistemic modals, is not required for a circumstantial reading, and has a distribution similar to subjunctive marking in other Salish languages (§4.2.3). Overall, this points towards there being a zero circumstantial modal in Nsyilcxn. This has already been argued for other Indigenous languages (Matthewson 2013 for Gitksan, Hannon 2025 for nɬeʔkepmxcín). This also points towards an analysis of cakʷ as a mood marker, rather than a modal proper.
This paper has shown several things.

gloss: Thompson River Salish, cited from Hannon 2025

form: First, nsyilxcn epistemic modals do not have an inherent temporal orientation, but rather rely on overt and zero sentential aspect to provide that orientation (Rullmann & Matthewson 2018). The temporal orientation of epistemic cəm̓/cmay depends on the aspectual properties of the inflected predicate, in other words . This means that in the abscence of overt prospective marking, a zero prospective is necessary to provide a future TO to cəm̓/cmay (see Kratzer 2011 for English, Louie 2015 for Blackfoot). nsyilxcn and nɬeʔkepmxcín (Hannon 2025) both have constructions whereby a modal has a future orientation even in the absence of prospective marking. The nsyilxcn pattern suggests that the nɬeʔkepmxcín pattern could plausibly be due to a zero prospective. Additionally, for prospective sentences without cəm̓/cmay, an epistemic interpretation is not available. This suggests that the nsyilxcn prospective (overt and null) is non -modal, and that there is no zero epistemic modal.

Second, bouletic particle cakʷ can be used in a range of different circumstantial contexts that coincide with the goals/desires of the speaker. Since (i) cakʷ can co-occur with epistemic cəm̓/cmay, (ii) cakʷ is unnecessary for a circumstantial reading, (iii) cakʷ is disallowed in some circumstantial contexts which do not coincide with the speaker’s goals/desires, and (iv) cakʷ converges with subjunctive marking in other Salish languages (Matthewson 2010), I propose that cakʷ is a mood marker, and I posit a zero circumstantial modal (see Matthewson 2013 on Gitksan, and Hannon 2025 for a similar claim for nɬeʔkepmxcín) whose force is contextually determined. Third, given that circumstantial modals always have a future temporal orientation (Condoravdi 2002, Rullmann & Matthewson 2018), yet both cakʷ and the zero circumstantial modal may co- occur with non -prospective aspects in nsyilxcn, sentential aspect is not providing the temporal orientation to the circumstantial modal.
Though certain questions remain before I am ready to propose a full formal analysis, I provide some initial thoughts here.

form: Copley (2009) claims that offers require a modal semantics. Glougie (2007) shows that in St’át’imcets, prospective cuz’ cannot be used for making an offer, while kelh can. (kelh and cuz’ may co-occur in an offer.) Conversely, only cuz’ is acceptable in cases where an event is already planned at utterance time, not kelh (see also Matthewson & Davis 2016). For these reasons Glougie analyzes kelh as a modal that occurs with non-future tense (Matthewson 2006) (thus allowing future and future-in-the-past readings), and which places the reference time after the evaluation time. cuz’ in contrast is a non-modal prospective aspect, which places the event time after the reference time (Abusch 1985). Hannon (2025) reaches a similar conclusion regarding n ɬeʔkepmxcín xʷúy̓, as a non-modal prospective aspect, which can co -occur with overt epistemic, or an overt or zero circumstantial modal.

nsyilxcn prospective markers mi, k- and the zero prospective may all be used in offer contexts, and regardless of whether an event has already been planned at utterance time or not. While this is consistent with the idea that these elements are more similar to St’át’imcets kelh, and should be analyzed as non-future modals (see also Matthewson 2013 for Gitksan) albeit ones which do not require that a plan for the eventuality overlaps with reference time (Copley 2014) , these might equally well be analyzed as non -modal prospectives which co -occur with a zero or overt modal (Matthewson 2013, Hannon 2025) . Recall that nsyilxcn shows evidence that modal sentences without overt modal particles cannot be interpreted epistemically, only circumstantially, regardless of aspect. This suggests not only a zero circumstantial modal, but assuming that this zero modal is always present in offer contexts as well as other circumstantial contexts but not in non - circumstantial contexts (which are simple prospectives), then there is no need to treat mi, k-, and the zero prospective as modal prospectives. In fact, a modal treatment of prospectivity in nsyilxcn, would require the modal base to be underspecified, and later disambiguated by a zero circumstantial or epistemic cəm̓/cmay. Thus, it seems that nsyilxcn prospective morphemes more closely resemble nɬeʔkepmxcín xʷuy̓ in the sense that they are non-modal (Hannon 2025), yet may co-occur with epistemic and (zero) circumstantial modals.

gloss: cited from Rullmann & Matthewson 2018, printed here without its acute

form: Regarding temporal orientation, Rullmann & Matthewson (2018) note that i n St’at’imcets, epistemic sentences require prospective marking for a future TO, which is argued to be evidence that the prospective marker supplies the modal with its future TO, while circumstantials disallow prospective marking , which is taken to be evidence that circumstantial modals are inherently prospective (due to a diversity condition, Condoravdi 2002). While epistemic modals in nsyilxcn clearly receive their TO from overt or zero sentential aspect (like St’át’imcets and n ɬeʔkepmxcín epistemic modals), this is less clear for the zero circumstantial modal. Given that there is a zero circumstantial modal in nsyilxcn and that circumstantial modals are are always future-oriented, we need to ask whether there must necessarily be a zero circumstantial modal in non -prospective sentences with a circumstantial modal flavour.

I suspect the answer is ‘no’. Examples (96)-(103) above lack any overt modal particle, but are plausibly all future -oriented, and so by hypothesis require the zero or overt prospective. On the other hand, the examples in §4.2.2 involve non-prospective aspect, but also all involve cakʷ. The generalization seems to be that while zero-marked predicates can be interpreted as both prospective and modal given a circumstantial context, they will not be interpreted as non-prospective and modal in the absence of cakʷ or cəm̓/cmay, only as non-modal non-prospectives. To put it in simpler terms, the zero circumstantial modal is only recoverable with prospectives. Given that cakʷ is largely optional in most circumstantial contexts for which I posit a zero circumstantial modal, it would be unexpected if the zero circumstantial modal required cakʷ only in non -prospective contexts. It seems more straightforward to assume that the zero circumstantial modal is only recoverable with prospectives because it does not occur with non -prospectives. This places the zero circumstantial modal in nsyilxcn in line with other Salish circumstantial modals.

This approach raises another question howe ver: Assuming that cakʷ is a mood marker, it may be understood as placing a presupposition on the modal accessibility relation R , such that R is bouletic (Portner 1997 , Matthewson 2010 ). This makes s ense given that similar to St’át’imcets subjunctive marking, cakʷ allows deontic, bouletic, and epistemic uses, and so is not restricted to a particular type of conversational background. But t his also means that cakʷ requires that its argument, or the proposition it modifies, be modalized. In prospective cases, for which there is a zero circumstantial modal, this presupposition is satisfied. How then can cakʷ be used in non - prospective cases, for which there is by hypothesis no zero circumstantial modal? Presupposition accommodation, or an analysis of cakʷ as embedding a zero subjunctive, are two possibilities that come to mind, though at present their potential remains unclear. In any case, the way forward must be able to address the non-bouletic uses of cakʷ (including counterfactual uses), and include a better understanding of how the equivalent of subjunctives in other Salish lan guages are realized in nsyilxcn.
